name: Swish
subcategory: macOS window management via trackpad gestures
tagline: A macOS menu bar utility that snaps, resizes and manages windows with two-finger swipes on the title bar.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as a one-time Mac purchase rather than a subscription.

verdictSummary: The boring half of this is genuinely easy: a Swift menu bar app that uses the Accessibility API to snap the focused window into halves, quarters and thirds is a single session of work. The interesting half is the input layer, and that is where one-shot builds die. Swish reads two-finger swipes and pinches on a window's title bar, disambiguates them from scrolling and dragging, and does it fast enough that it feels like a system feature rather than a script, which means fighting NSEvent monitors, gesture thresholds and per-app title bar weirdness. An agent will get you keyboard-shortcut window snapping that works, plus a wobbly gesture prototype that misfires often enough that you stop using it. Budget a weekend and accept that the feel is the product and the feel is what you will be missing.
coreLoopDIY: A menu bar app that grabs the focused window through the Accessibility API and snaps or resizes it into a grid position, triggered by global keyboard shortcuts and a best-effort two-finger swipe listener.
requirements: Swift and a willingness to read AppKit docs from 2013
Accessibility permission granted to your unsigned binary
A local ad-hoc signing setup, or an Apple developer account if you want it to survive updates
whatYouLose: Gesture feel: threshold tuning, direction disambiguation and cancel behaviour that took years of user complaints to get right
Reliable title bar hit testing across apps that draw their own chrome, Electron apps, full screen windows and multi-monitor setups with mixed scaling
The extra gestures beyond snapping: tab switching, window closing, minimising, app switching, Mission Control
A signed, notarised, auto-updating build that does not silently lose Accessibility permission after every rebuild
Low idle CPU and no beachballs, which is harder than it sounds when you are monitoring every trackpad event
moatNotes: The moat is entirely in the input layer. Nobody buys a window manager for its feature list, they buy it because the gesture fires exactly when they meant it to.
whyPeopleStillPay: It is a one-time purchase for a utility you touch a hundred times a day, and the DIY version has an unusually annoying failure mode: a window manager that misreads gestures is worse than no window manager, because it moves things you did not want moved. Paying once buys you someone else's years of edge case handling against Electron apps, external monitors and macOS releases that quietly change Accessibility behaviour. If you only want keyboard snapping, build it and never look back. If you want the trackpad part, the price is roughly one hour of your time.
notes: The snapping is a Saturday afternoon; the gesture recognition is the whole app.
prompt:
Build a macOS menu bar window manager in Swift. No cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Swift 5.9+, AppKit for the menu bar and window control, SwiftUI only for the small settings window.
- Xcode project, macOS 13+ target, local ad-hoc signing. No App Store target.
- Zero third-party dependencies except HotKey (or hand-rolled Carbon RegisterEventHotKey if you prefer).

Core behaviour:
- Request Accessibility permission on first launch, with a clear prompt and a button that opens System Settings to the right pane.
- Use AXUIElement to read and set the frame of the frontmost window of the frontmost app.
- Implement snap targets: left half, right half, top half, bottom half, four quarters, left/center/right thirds, maximise, center, and restore-previous-frame.
- Keep a per-window undo stack (last 3 frames) keyed by window identity so restore actually works.
- Global keyboard shortcuts for every target, user-editable in settings, persisted to UserDefaults.
- Multi-display aware: snap relative to the screen containing the window, respecting visibleFrame and menu bar/Dock insets.

Gesture layer, best effort and clearly marked experimental:
- Install an NSEvent global monitor for .scrollWheel with hasPreciseScrollingDeltas, plus .magnify.
- Only act when the cursor is inside the frontmost window's title bar region, computed from the AX frame minus content area height.
- Two-finger swipe left/right snaps to that half, swipe up maximises, swipe down restores.
- Require a minimum accumulated delta before firing, then lock out further gestures for 400ms.
- Add a settings toggle to disable gestures entirely, defaulting to on.

Explicitly out of scope: tab switching gestures, Mission Control or Spaces manipulation, licensing, auto-update, notarisation, app-specific workarounds, animation of window movement.

Deliver a README that lists the shortcuts, states the known gesture false-positive cases honestly, and gives the exact command to build and run.
